text.what: A plain earthenware bowl with writing inside it. The text is inked in a spiral that starts at the rim and winds inward to the centre, most often in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, sometimes Mandaic, Syriac, Arabic or Persian. Then the bowl is turned upside down and buried — under a threshold, in a courtyard, in the corner of a house where somebody has just died, in a cemetery. Around one in ten carries no real language at all.
text.story:
John Charles Arnold sets out the mechanism the way its users described it: "When placed upside down under each corner of a house, demons would follow the inscribed charms that spiraled from the outer rim inward, only to be caught in the center."

The bowls belong to Sasanian Mesopotamia, sixth to eighth century, in a population that was Christian, Manichaean, Mandaean, Jewish, Zoroastrian or still Babylonian in religion, and largely Aramaic-speaking whatever else it was. They were commissioned across those lines. Nearly eighty Jewish bowls survive from Babylon under Sasanian rule, most from the Jewish settlement at Nippur, where almost every excavated house had them buried in it. They name what they are against: the evil eye, Lilith, Bagdana. Their inscriptions quote scripture and rabbinic texts alike, which scholars read as evidence that the rabbinic material was held to carry the same power as the biblical.

Two things follow that are worth stating plainly. The bowls often call themselves amulets, and the Talmud, which was being written in the same place and period, discusses the use of amulets to drive away demons — so the text on these bowls is the only written material documenting Jewish language and religion recovered from that time and place. And the corpus is a scandal: about 2,000 bowls are registered as archaeological finds, while the trade digs them up freely, so there may be tens of thousands in private hands.

There is an Islamic branch. In the medieval period, talismanic bowls did the same work in metal rather than clay, covered in Arabic — Qur'anic verses, a hadith, sometimes numerology or astrology — and used for healing by drinking water left standing in them overnight.

dating.label: 6th to 8th century CE
dating.note: The Jewish bowls are dated by the Sasanian period of the Nippur settlement (226–636); the Mandaic bowls from Nippur run into the early Islamic era.

object.made_by: scribes writing to commission, across religious lines; about ten per cent of the bowls are in pseudo-script and are thought to be the work of scribes who could not write, sold to clients who could not read
object.inscription: a spiral incantation from rim to centre, naming the household and the demons it is aimed at, and quoting scripture and rabbinic texts
object.script: Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, Mandaic, Syriac; a handful in Arabic or Persian
object.note: Form is a household bowl; there is no bowl key in the vocabulary yet.
